sd0-t4.title: The building blocks of a web system, and one request through them

frames.caption: Most web systems are built from the same dozen parts. Follow one photo upload through them — each box is a later topic, close up.
DNS: the app asks for the address of api.example.com and gets back an IP address — like looking up a phone number.
The request reaches the load balancer, which picks one of many identical app servers that is healthy and not too busy.
The app server runs your code: it checks who the user is, gets an upload link from object storage, and saves the caption and photo details in the database — the source of truth.
Slow work goes on a queue: "make thumbnails for photo 42". The app server replies straight away; a background worker does the job later.
When friends open the post, the app server checks the cache (fast memory) first, and only reads the database on a miss.
The photo itself comes from a CDN server near each friend — not from your servers. On a miss, the CDN fetches it once from object storage.
Netflix, Instagram and a small startup all share this shape. What changes is the size of each box, and which boxes matter most.

sd0-t1.title: A step-by-step answer to any design question

frames.caption: Interviewers grade how you think. A fixed order of steps stops you jumping straight to boxes and arrows. Here is the order, run on "Design a URL shortener".
1 Requirements: ask what it must do and how well. Write the answers in a corner of the board.
2 Estimates: turn the numbers into load. 100 million new links a month is about 39 writes a second; at 100 reads per write, about 4000 reads a second. Say each assumption out loud.
3 API: two or three endpoints fix exactly what the system must do.
4 Data model: the main tables and their keys. The main query is "code → long URL", so code is the key.
5 Design: draw the simplest thing that works, and walk one request through it. Make it work before you make it big.
6 Deep dive: go where your estimates point. Reads dominate, so cache hot codes; and the hard part is making short codes unique — a counter turned into Base62.
7 Wrap-up: the design in three sentences, its weak spots, and what you would monitor. Then stop — let them ask.

sd0-t2.title: Turn users into requests per second, storage and bandwidth

frames.caption: Rough numbers decide the design. Start from users: 10 million a day, each reading 20 pages and posting 1 item.
A day has 86,400 seconds — call it 100,000. So 200 M reads a day is about 2,000 a second; 10 M writes a day is about 100 a second.
Traffic is not flat: the peak is often 2–5 times the average. Design for the peak.
Storage: 10 M posts a day × 1 KB = 10 GB a day, about 3.6 TB a year — about 11 TB with 3 copies.
Bandwidth: 2,000 reads a second × 100 KB = 200 MB a second going out. Now decide: one database or many? Does the hot data fit in a cache? Is a CDN needed?

shapes.text: one DB or many?  cache?  CDN?

sd0-t3.title: A low-level design answer, step by step

frames.caption: 1 Clarify: write the use cases as short sentences, and agree what is out of scope.
2 Find the entities: the nouns become candidate classes; the verbs (assign, pay) become methods.
3 Draw the class diagram: fields, key methods and relationships. For each line ask: is it "is-a" or "has-a"?
4 Spot what varies — pricing rules, how a spot is chosen — and put each behind an interface (Strategy).
5 Code the main flow, park(): the lot asks its SpotAssigner for a free spot, marks it taken and issues a ticket.
6 Stress-test it: two cars at two gates want the same spot at the same moment. Claiming a spot must be one atomic step, so only one gate wins.

shapes.text: claim the spot atomically: one gate wins

sd1-t1.title: Typing a URL: find the server, connect, ask, answer

frames.caption: You type example.com. The browser checks its own DNS cache, then the operating system's. Both miss.
It asks a resolver, usually run by your internet provider.
The resolver asks a root server: "who handles .com?" The root points it at the .com servers.
It asks a .com server: "who handles example.com?" It is pointed at example.com's own name server.
The name server returns the IP address: 203.0.113.10. Every answer along the way is cached for its TTL, so next time is much quicker.
With the IP address, the browser opens a TCP connection on port 443: a three-step handshake — SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.
TLS handshake: the server shows a certificate proving it really is example.com, and both sides agree on encryption keys.
Now the request: "GET /", with "Host: example.com". The load balancer passes it to one of many app servers.
The app server reads the cache or database, builds the page and sends it back.
The browser then requests the images, CSS and scripts — often from a CDN close to you.

sd1-t2.title: A predictable API: clear resources, honest status codes, safe retries

frames.caption: The app creates an order: POST /v1/orders, with an Idempotency-Key header — a random id for this one attempt.
The server creates order 981 and stores the key with the result. It replies 201 Created…
…but the reply is lost on a bad network. The app cannot tell whether the order was made, so it retries with the SAME key.
The server finds k7 already stored and returns the same result: order 981. No second order. POST isn't idempotent by itself — the key makes the retry safe.
Lists are paginated. GET /v1/orders?limit=20 returns 20 orders and a cursor pointing at where the page ended.
200 OK: 20 orders plus cursor=abc.
The app sends the cursor back for the next 20. Methods mean what they say (GET reads), and the URL names a resource (/orders), not a verb.

sd1-t3.title: Getting the server to push: polling, long polling, WebSockets, SSE

frames.caption: Normal HTTP: the client asks, the server answers. For chat, live scores or notifications, the server needs a way to push.
Short polling: ask "anything new?" every few seconds. Simple — but most answers are "no", and each one costs a full request.
Long polling: ask, and the server holds the request open until there is news (or about 30 s pass). The client immediately asks again.
WebSocket: starts as an HTTP request with an Upgrade header; then the same connection stays open and either side can send at any time.
SSE (server-sent events): one HTTP request, and the server keeps sending events down it. One-way, simpler, and the browser reconnects by itself.
At scale, users connect to many gateway servers. A registry (such as Redis) records which gateway holds each user.
A sends a message to B over its open connection to gateway 1.
Gateway 1 asks the registry where B is connected: gateway 2.
It forwards the message to gateway 2, which pushes it down B's open connection.

sd1-t4.title: A CDN serves copies from somewhere near the user

frames.caption: cdn.example.com points at the CDN. A user's request goes to the nearest edge server, found through DNS or anycast routing.
Cache miss: the edge doesn't have the file yet, so it fetches it from your origin — once — across the world.
It stores a copy and returns it. This first request was slow, but it paid for everyone after it.
Cache hit: the next user in Tokyo gets the file from the edge in a few milliseconds. Your servers never see the request.
The copy stays until its TTL runs out. Less latency for users, less load on you, and spikes are absorbed at the edge.

sd1-t5.title: One front door that checks, limits and routes every request

frames.caption: Clients send every request to one address, api.example.com, instead of knowing about every service.
The gateway handles TLS, then checks the token (who is this?)…
…and the rate limit (are they allowed this many requests?).
It routes by path: /orders/… goes to the order service. (Behind it, a load balancer picks one copy of that service.)
It waits for the answer, sends it back, and logs the request and how long it took. Business logic stays in the services, not the gateway.

sd2-t1.title: Scaling up (a bigger machine) versus scaling out (more machines)

frames.caption: Vertical scaling: when one server is too slow, buy a bigger one — more CPU, more memory. Nothing else changes.
Simple, and it often works for a long time.
But there is a ceiling — the biggest machine you can buy — and it is still ONE machine. If it fails, everything is down.

shapes.text: the biggest machine money can buy

frames.caption: Horizontal scaling: more machines instead of a bigger one. First find the bottleneck — CPU, database, memory or network.
The key trick: make app servers stateless. Login sessions move out of server memory into a shared store (Redis), so any server can handle any user.
Now just add servers behind the load balancer. With auto-scaling they are added when CPU or latency rises.
A server dies? The others carry on — no single point of failure. Take reads off the database with caches and replicas; shard it when writes become the bottleneck.

sd2-t2.title: Availability: counting the nines, and how redundancy adds them

frames.caption: Availability is the share of time the system works. 99% sounds good — but it allows 3.65 days of downtime a year.
99.9%: 8.8 hours a year. Each extra nine cuts downtime tenfold — and costs much more than the one before.
99.99%: 53 minutes a year. Each extra nine cuts downtime tenfold — and costs much more than the one before.
99.999%: 5.3 minutes a year. Each extra nine cuts downtime tenfold — and costs much more than the one before.
Two parts in series — a request needs BOTH: 99.9% × 99.9% = 99.8%. Every part you add in series lowers the total.
Two redundant copies in parallel — EITHER will do: 1 − 0.01 × 0.01 = 99.99%, from two copies that are each only 99%. That is why you remove single points of failure.
…as long as the copies fail independently. Put them in different availability zones, check their health every few seconds, and fail over automatically. Then practise the failover.

sd2-t3.title: Staying up when something fails: timeouts, backoff, circuit breakers

frames.caption: Never wait forever: give each call a timeout — 300 ms here. The first call is too slow, so it is abandoned.
The failure looks temporary and the call is safe to repeat, so retry — but wait first. Exponential backoff: about 100 ms, then 200, then 400. Here: 87 ms.
Each wait doubles, plus a little randomness (jitter) — 178 ms, then 370 ms — so many clients retrying at once don't all hit the service at the same instant.
Checkout calls a recommendations service through a circuit breaker. Closed: calls pass straight through.
Recommendations slows down. The breaker counts failures: half the calls in the last 10 seconds have timed out…
…so it OPENS: for the next 30 seconds every call fails instantly, without touching the struggling service. It gets room to recover.
Meanwhile checkout uses a fallback: the page loads without recommendations, or with cached ones. Checkout itself stays fast.
After the wait: HALF-OPEN. A few test calls go through. They succeed, so the breaker CLOSES and normal service resumes. (If they had failed, it would open again.)

sd2-t4.title: Load balancing: spread the work, skip the broken servers

frames.caption: Clients only ever see the load balancer's address. It makes many servers look like one.
Round robin: request 1 goes to the next server in turn — server 1.
Round robin: request 2 goes to the next server in turn — server 2.
Round robin: request 3 goes to the next server in turn — server 3.
Every few seconds it calls each server's /health endpoint. Server 2 fails a few checks in a row, so it is taken out of the rotation.
Request 4 → server 3. Traffic goes only to healthy servers; server 2 is added back when it recovers.
Request 5 → server 1. Traffic goes only to healthy servers; server 2 is added back when it recovers.
Least connections: the balancer tracks how many requests each server is busy with right now.
A new request goes to the least busy server — server 2 — which is fairer when some requests take much longer than others.
A layer 7 balancer can also read the request itself — path, headers, cookies — and route /api to API servers and /images to a media service.

sd2-t5.title: Cache-aside: check the cache, fall back to the database, keep them in step

frames.caption: A request needs product 42. Cache-aside: ask the cache first, for the key "product:42".
Miss: it isn't there. Read the database instead — perhaps 5–20 ms.
Return the result, and store it in the cache with a TTL of, say, 5 minutes.
The next read is a hit: under a millisecond, and the database never sees it.
Product 42 changes. Write the database, then DELETE the cache key, so the next read loads the fresh value. Keeping the cache in step is the hard part (invalidation).
When the cache is full it evicts keys — usually the least recently used. Watch the hit rate: 95% means only 1 read in 20 reaches the database.

sd2-t6.title: When copies can't talk: choose consistency or availability

frames.caption: Two copies of one account, in London and Paris. Both say £100, and they keep each other in step.
The network between them breaks: a partition. It WILL happen sooner or later. Now a user in London withdraws £80.
A CP system (consistent) refuses, because it can't confirm with Paris. Always correct — but some requests fail until the network heals.
An AP system (available) accepts: London now says £20 while Paris still says £100. Both keep answering — but a second £80 withdrawal in Paris would overdraw the account.
When the network heals, the AP system must reconcile the two copies. So during a partition the real choice is consistency OR availability.
PACELC adds: Else, with no partition, waiting for both copies before saying "done" is consistent but slower. Even on a good day you trade latency against consistency.

sd2-t7.title: A token bucket: bursts allowed, abuse refused

frames.caption: Token bucket: each user has a bucket holding up to 10 tokens, refilled at 1 token a second.
Second 0: a burst of 6 requests. Each takes a token; all 6 go through. Short bursts are fine. 4 tokens left.
Second 1: the bucket has refilled to 5. 6 more requests: 5 get tokens; then the bucket is empty, so the rest (1) get 429 Too Many Requests, with "Retry-After: 1".
Second 4: after a quiet spell the bucket has refilled to 3, so the user's next 3 requests go through. Sustained abuse is held to 1 a second; normal use never notices.

With many gateway servers, each bucket lives in Redis and is updated atomically, so every server shares one count. Inside the system, backpressure does the same job: a full queue stops accepting new work instead of growing forever.

sd2-t8.title: A queue lets the API answer now and do the slow work later

frames.caption: A user uploads a video. The API stores the file and puts a message, {video_id: 42}, on a queue.
The API replies straight away — "202 Accepted, processing" — instead of making the user wait for the conversion.
Workers pull messages at their own pace. Worker 1 takes message 42 and starts converting the video.
Worker 1 crashes before it finishes. It never acknowledged the message, so the queue makes it visible again…
…and worker 2 picks it up and retries. Only when a worker acknowledges the message is it removed for good.
A message that fails too many times goes to a dead-letter queue for a person to inspect, instead of blocking everything behind it.
10,000 uploads at once? They simply wait in the queue — it absorbs the spike. Add workers to clear it faster.

sd2-t9.title: Metrics say when, traces say where, logs say why

frames.caption: Metrics: the p99 checkout latency jumps from 300 ms to 2 s and stays there. An alert fires — on a symptom users feel, not on a CPU blip.

shapes.text: ALERT: p99 above SLO for 5 min

frames.caption: Traces: the first service created a trace ID and passed it in a header to every service it called. Each records how long its part took.
Laid out as a waterfall, one bar stands out: the payment service takes about 1.7 s…
…and almost all of it is one database call: about 1.6 s.
Logs: that service's structured logs for trace 7f3a show why — a lock timeout. Metrics said WHEN, the trace said WHERE, the logs said WHY.

sd3-t1.title: Choosing a database: match the store to the data and its queries

frames.caption: Start from the data and its main queries, not from the product names. There are five broad shapes of database.
Need joins, transactions and flexible queries over structured data — "a user's last 20 orders", "revenue by month"? Start with SQL.
One simple lookup by key dominates, and must be extremely fast or enormous — a shopping cart by id? A key-value store.
Each record is a self-contained document whose fields vary from one to the next? A document store.
Massive writes, always read by one key in order — "all messages in a chat, by time"? A wide-column store.
The questions are about relationships — "friends of friends who like X"? A graph database.
Real systems mix them. An online shop: orders and payments in PostgreSQL, carts in a key-value store, product search in Elasticsearch, "people also bought" precomputed or in a graph.

sd3-t2.title: A transaction: all of it happens, or none of it does

frames.caption: Transfer £100 from A to B. BEGIN starts a transaction: from here on it is all or nothing.
Take £100 from A — only if A has it (a rule the database checks: Consistent). Other users can't see this yet (Isolated).
Add £100 to B. Each change is also written to a write-ahead log on disk.
COMMIT: the log is saved to disk, and only then is success reported. Both changes become visible together (Atomic), and survive a crash (Durable).
Same transfer. Take £100 from A…
…and the server crashes before COMMIT.
On restart, the database replays its log. This transaction never committed, so every change in it is undone: A is back to £300. No money vanished — Atomic.

sd3-t3.title: An index: a sorted tree that finds a row in a few steps

frames.caption: WHERE email = 'kim@x.io' with no index: the database reads every row and checks it — a full table scan.
CREATE INDEX on email builds a B-tree: the emails, sorted, in a shallow tree. Leaves hold every email with a pointer to its row; the root holds signposts.
Start at the root: "kim@x.io" sorts between the signposts, so take the middle branch. Each step down cuts the search space enormously.
In the leaf, find the email, and follow its pointer to the row. With 100 million rows the tree is only 4–5 levels deep: a handful of reads instead of millions.
The cost: every INSERT — and every UPDATE of an email — must also update the tree. Indexes make reads fast and writes slower, and they take space.

sd3-t4.title: Replication: copies on several machines, and what lag looks like

frames.caption: All writes go to the leader. A user changes their profile name from "Sam" to "Samir".
The leader saves it and adds it to its replication log. Followers read that log and apply the same changes, in the same order.
Follower 1 is synchronous: the leader waits for it to confirm before telling the client "done". Safe — but every write waits.
Follower 2 is asynchronous and a little behind. The user refreshes, the read goes to follower 2… and shows the OLD name. That is replication lag.
Fix: "read your own writes" — for a short time after a write, send that user's reads to the leader. Follower 2 catches up a moment later anyway.
The leader dies. The followers notice: its heartbeats stop arriving.
Pick the most up-to-date follower — follower 1 has log entry #91 — and promote it to be the new leader.
Writes now go to the new leader, and follower 2 copies from it. The system is back, having lost nothing that was confirmed.

sd3-t5.title: Sharding: split the data by a key, and route each query

frames.caption: One database can't hold all the writes, so the data is split into shards by a key — user_id. A routing rule picks the shard: hash(user_id) % 3.
User 42: hash(42) % 3 = 1, so all of user 42's data lives on shard 1.
User 17: hash(17) % 3 = 2, so all of user 17's data lives on shard 2.
User 8: hash(8) % 3 = 0, so all of user 8's data lives on shard 0.
User 23: hash(23) % 3 = 0, so all of user 23's data lives on shard 0.
"Show user 42's profile" goes to exactly one shard — fast. That is why the shard key should match the main query.
"Count all users who signed up today" has no single key, so it must ask EVERY shard and merge the answers. Cross-shard queries are slow.
Range sharding instead: names A–H on shard 0, I–Q on shard 1, R–Z on shard 2. Neighbouring keys stay together, so range queries are easy.

But traffic is rarely even. A popular stretch of keys — say, new sign-ups whose ids all sort together — lands on one shard: a hot spot. Hash sharding spreads keys evenly, at the cost of range queries.

shapes.text: one shard does most of the work

sd3-t6.title: Consistent hashing: adding a server moves only a few keys

frames.caption: The simple way to pick a server: hash(key) % N. With 4 servers, each key gets server 0, 1, 2 or 3 — shown on each key.
Add one server and N becomes 5: hash(key) % 5 gives most keys a DIFFERENT server (11 of these 16, outlined). Measured on 1,000 keys: 81% move — for a cache, nearly every entry lost at once.
Consistent hashing puts servers AND keys on a ring. Each key belongs to the next server clockwise — its colour shows which.
Add server E. It only takes the keys between itself and the server before it (A). Outlined keys are the ones that moved; every other key stays put.
Measured on 1,000 keys: 19% move with the ring, against 81% with % N. Virtual nodes — each server placed at many points — keep the load even.

sd3-t7.title: Big files go to object storage; the database keeps only the key

frames.caption: Databases are bad at holding big files. The app asks your API: "I want to upload a profile photo."
The API checks the user, then asks object storage for a pre-signed URL: a link that allows ONE upload, to ONE key, for a few minutes.
The app uploads the file straight to that URL. Your servers never touch the bytes.
The API saves only a small row: users/42/avatar.jpg, the owner, size and time. The database keeps the key; the storage keeps the file.
To show the photo, the app uses a CDN URL for that key (or a short-lived signed link for private files). Fast downloads, and no load on your servers.

sd3-t8.title: An inverted index: from each word to the documents that contain it

frames.caption: LIKE '%shoe%' would read every row. A search engine does the work in advance. Three product titles:
Indexing: split each title into words, lowercase them, and reduce them to stems — "Running" → "run", "Shoes" → "shoe".
For each word, keep a posting list: the documents it appears in. This is the inverted index — like a cookbook's index of ingredients.
Search "red shoes": stem the query the same way (red, shoe), then look up each word's list — no scan at all.
Intersect the lists: documents with both words → 1. Each match is then scored — rare words that are frequent in this document score higher (TF-IDF, BM25).

sd3-t9.title: Snowflake IDs: time, machine and a counter in one 64-bit number

frames.caption: One auto-increment counter is a bottleneck at scale. A Snowflake ID is built from three parts in one 64-bit number, so every machine can make IDs on its own.
The timestamp comes first: milliseconds since a chosen start date (1,234,567,890). Because it leads, later IDs are bigger, so they sort roughly by time.
Then the machine ID, 37, given out when the machine starts — so two machines can never make the same ID.
Another ID in the same millisecond: the sequence goes up by one — 0, 1, 2 … up to 4,095. If it runs out, wait for the next millisecond.
Next millisecond: the timestamp moves on and the sequence starts again at 0. The new ID is bigger than every earlier one — unique, roughly ordered, and made locally.

sd4-t1.title: From one app to services — one boundary at a time

frames.caption: A monolith: one app, deployed as one piece, with one database. Simple to build, test and deploy — a good place to start, if it is well organised inside.
Split gradually, around business capabilities. Carve out ONE service at a time — orders first — with its own database. Other services may only use its API or its events.
When an order is placed, the order service publishes "order placed" and moves on. Things that can happen later go through events…
…and the payment and notification services react on their own. Each team deploys and scales its service independently.
The price: a function call is now a network call that can be slow or fail, data is spread across databases, and you need tracing, a gateway and a pipeline per service.

sd4-t2.title: Sagas undo with compensations; the outbox never loses an event

frames.caption: Across services there is no single ACID transaction. A saga runs the steps one by one, each a local transaction: reserve stock, charge the card, create the shipment.
Step 1: "reserve stock". The stock service reserves it and replies OK.
Step 2: "charge the card". The card is declined.
So the orchestrator runs compensations, in reverse order, for every step that succeeded: "release the stock".
The order is marked FAILED and the user is told. Shipping was never asked. Every service is back in a consistent state — without a global lock.
"Save the order AND publish an event" is two systems — a crash in between loses the event. The outbox pattern fixes that.
In ONE local transaction, the service writes the order row and an "OrderCreated" row into an outbox table. Both are saved, or neither is.
A relay process reads new outbox rows…
…and publishes them to Kafka, retrying until it succeeds, then marks them sent. The event can never be lost — at worst it is sent twice, so consumers must be idempotent.

sd4-t3.title: Raft: elect a leader by majority, commit what a majority holds

frames.caption: Three nodes must agree on one leader and one order of changes. Every node starts as a follower, waiting to hear from a leader.
Node 1 hears nothing for its random timeout (say 150–300 ms), so it becomes a candidate for term 2 and asks the others for their votes.
Each node votes once per term. With votes from a majority — 2 of 3, counting its own — node 1 becomes leader and starts sending heartbeats.
A client write goes to the leader. It adds "x = 5" to its log and sends the entry to the followers.
Node 2 stores it. Now a majority (2 of 3) have the entry, so it is COMMITTED and applied, even though node 3 is slow.
The leader dies. Heartbeats stop, a follower times out, and a new election begins for term 3. With 3 nodes the cluster survives 1 failure — a majority is still possible.

sd4-t4.title: Who are you, and what may you do: login, tokens and checks

frames.caption: Log in: the password travels over HTTPS. The server hashes it with the user's stored salt and compares with the stored hash — passwords are never stored in plain text.
It matches (and the one-time code is valid), so the server issues a short-lived access token (15 minutes) and a longer-lived refresh token.
Every request carries the access token. The gateway checks its signature and expiry — no database call needed. That is authentication: who are you?
The payments service then checks authorisation: does THIS user own account 123? It checks on the server, every time — never trusting the app.
After 15 minutes the access token expires; the app swaps the refresh token for a new one. Logging out revokes the refresh token, so the session really ends.

sd5-t1.title: The four pillars, on one bank account

frames.caption: A class groups data and behaviour: a BankAccount holds a balance and has deposit() and withdraw().
Encapsulation: the balance is private (–). Nobody can set it to −£30 directly. withdraw(80) checks there is enough money first, and refuses.
Abstraction: callers only see deposit(), withdraw() and the balance — not how interest, fees or the ledger work inside.
Inheritance: a SavingsAccount IS a BankAccount that also adds interest. It reuses everything and adds one thing.
Polymorphism: code loops over all accounts calling monthly_update(). Each type does the right thing — savings add interest, current accounts take a fee — and the loop never asks which is which.

sd5-t2.title: Composition: build behaviour from parts instead of subclasses

frames.caption: With inheritance, every combination of behaviours needs its own subclass: 3 ways to fly × 3 sounds = 9 classes — and every new behaviour multiplies them again.
With composition, a Duck simply HOLDS a flying object and a quacking object. Each behaviour is a small class behind a tiny interface: fly() or quack().
Build a duck by choosing its parts: Duck(Wings(), Quack()). Six small classes cover all nine combinations.
A rubber duck is Duck(NoFly(), Squeak()) — no new subclass needed.
You can even swap a part while the program runs — strap a Rocket on — and test each part on its own. Inherit only for a true "is-a" with shared behaviour.

sd5-t3.title: Single responsibility: one class, one reason to change

frames.caption: One Invoice class calculates totals, saves itself to the database and emails itself. Three different people ask for changes to it.
Marketing asks for a new email layout. Editing send_email() in the same class risks breaking the totals — finance's code — by accident.
Split it: one class per reason to change. Invoice calculates, InvoiceRepository saves, InvoiceEmailer sends.
A small coordinating function calls them in order. Now an email change touches only InvoiceEmailer.

sd5-t4.title: Open/closed: add behaviour by adding classes, not editing old code

frames.caption: A price calculator that switches on the discount type with if/elif. Every new kind of discount means editing this method.
Adding a student discount means opening working code and adding another branch — risking the cases that already work.
Instead, depend on an interface: DiscountRule with apply(price). Each branch becomes its own small class; the calculator just asks every rule it is given.
A new discount is a new class. The calculator never changes: open for extension, closed for modification.

sd5-t5.title: Liskov: a subclass must keep its parent's promises

frames.caption: Code written for Rectangle relies on a promise: after set_width(5), the width is 5 and the height hasn't changed. Then set the height to 4: the area is 20.
Square inherits from Rectangle, and keeps its sides equal: set_height(4) ALSO sets the width to 4. The same code now gets 16 — the parent's promise is broken.
If calling code has to check "is this the special subclass?", Liskov is broken. Square isn't a true subtype of a CHANGEABLE Rectangle.
Fix the hierarchy: Rectangle and Square both implement a Shape interface with area(), and there are no setters that conflict. Every Shape keeps every promise of Shape.

sd5-t6.title: Interface segregation: small interfaces, nothing forced

frames.caption: One big Machine interface: print(), scan() and fax(). Every class that implements it must write all three.
A basic printer can only print, so it is forced to write empty methods that raise "not supported". A change to fax() still ripples into it.
Split the interface by what clients actually need: Printer, Scanner, Fax. Each is small.
BasicPrinter implements only Printer. An office machine implements all three. Nobody writes methods they don't support.

sd5-t7.title: Dependency inversion: depend on an interface, pass the details in

frames.caption: OrderService creates a PostgresRepository inside itself. The high-level business code now depends on a low-level detail.
So you can't swap the database, and you can't test OrderService without a real database running.
Invert it: define the interface the business code needs — OrderRepository with save(order). OrderService depends on that; PostgresRepository implements it. Both arrows now point at the abstraction.
The real repository is passed in at start-up. In tests, pass an in-memory one instead — no database needed. OrderService never changed.

sd5-t9.title: A race condition, and how a lock prevents it

frames.caption: One seat left. Two threads sell tickets at the same moment.
A reads seats_left = 1. B also reads seats_left = 1 — before A has written anything.
A sells the seat and writes 0. B, still believing there is 1 left, sells it too and writes 0. Two tickets for one seat — a lost update.
Fix: wrap "read, check, write" in a lock, so only one thread runs that critical section at a time.
A takes the lock, reads 1, sells, writes 0, and releases it. B has to wait.
Then B gets the lock, reads 0, and refuses. One seat, one ticket.
Across many servers a lock inside one program can't help. Do it in the database: UPDATE seats SET sold = true WHERE id = 7 AND sold = false — and check exactly one row changed.

sd6-t1.title: Singleton: exactly one instance — even with threads

frames.caption: A Singleton keeps one hidden instance and hands it out to everyone — a config object, say. get_instance() checks: is there one yet? If not, create it.
Without care, two threads can check at the same moment, both see "none yet"…
…and both create one. Now there are two "single" instances.
Fix: wrap creation in a lock, and check again inside it. Thread 1 creates the instance; thread 2 waits, checks again, finds it, and returns the same one.
The price: it is global state. It hides dependencies and makes tests share one object. Often it is cleaner to create one instance at start-up and pass it in.

sd6-t2.title: Factory: one place decides which class to create

frames.caption: Every notifier implements one interface: send(message). The decision "which class?" lives in ONE place — a factory holding a dictionary from name to class.
The order service asks the factory for "sms". It never writes SmsNotifier() itself.
The factory looks "sms" up and returns an SmsNotifier. The service only uses it through the interface: notifier.send("Your order shipped").
Adding WhatsApp means one new class and one new dictionary entry. No caller changes at all.

sd6-t3.title: Builder: set the parts by name, then build once

frames.caption: A request has many optional parts. A constructor with all of them in a row — Request(url, method, None, None, 5…) — is unreadable and easy to get wrong.
A builder sets each part with a clearly named method, starting from sensible defaults. Each method returns the builder, so the calls chain.
.method(…) sets one more part.
.header(…) sets one more part.
.body(…) sets one more part.
.timeout(…) sets one more part.
build() checks the combination is valid — the URL is set, the timeout is in range — then returns the finished object, which can be read-only.

sd6-t4.title: Adapter: translate between the interface you want and the one you have

frames.caption: Your code expects pay(amount_in_pounds) → True/False. A third-party bank SDK offers make_payment(pence, currency) → "OK" or an error code. They don't fit.
An adapter implements YOUR interface and holds the SDK. Your code calls pay(12.50) as usual.
The adapter converts the inputs — £12.50 → 1250 pence, currency "GBP" — and calls the SDK.
It converts the output back: "OK" becomes True. Your code never knew the SDK existed.
An error code like "E42" becomes a proper exception — PaymentDeclined — rather than being silently swallowed.

sd6-t5.title: Decorator: add features by wrapping, one layer each

frames.caption: Wrappers, one inside another: Logging(Caching(RealDataSource())). Each implements the same read() and holds the next one in.
A caller calls read(). The outer wrapper, Logging, writes a log line, then calls the object inside it.
Caching checks its cache: a miss, so it passes the call inward.
The real object does the work, and the answer travels back out through each wrapper — Caching keeps a copy on the way.
Call read() again: Caching answers from its copy and never bothers the real object. Callers can't tell any wrapper is there — they just call read().

sd6-t6.title: Facade: one simple method in front of a busy subsystem

frames.caption: Placing an order touches four subsystems, in the right order. Without help, every caller would repeat all those steps — and get the order wrong somewhere.
A facade offers ONE method for the common task: place_order(cart).
Reserve the stock: the facade calls inventory.reserve().
charge the card: the facade calls payment.charge().
create the shipment: the facade calls shipping.create().
send the confirmation: the facade calls notifications.send().
Callers make one call; advanced callers can still use the subsystems directly. Keep the facade thin, or it grows into a "god class".

sd6-t7.title: Strategy: swap the algorithm without touching its user

frames.caption: Instead of an if/elif on the pricing type inside Ride, each pricing rule is its own class with the same method: price(distance_km).
Ride holds one strategy and just calls it. Normal pricing for 10 km: £14.50.
Rush hour: swap the strategy at runtime — from configuration, a factory or the clock. Same Ride, same call: £26.10.
A new rule is a new class. Ride never changes, and each strategy can be tested on its own.

sd6-t8.title: Observer: publish once, every subscriber reacts

frames.caption: Several parts of the program care when an order is placed. Instead of the order code calling each one, they SUBSCRIBE: the subject keeps a list.
The event happens. The subject loops through its list and calls each subscriber with the details: "order 981 placed".
Each reacts in its own way: send an email, record a metric, reduce the stock. The order code doesn't know or care what they do.
A new reaction — loyalty points — just subscribes itself. The subject never changes. Subscribers can unsubscribe when they no longer care.

sd6-t9.title: Chain of responsibility: pass it along until someone handles it

frames.caption: Each handler decides: deal with the request, or pass it to the next handler it holds. The handlers are independent and can be reordered.
An expense of £60 goes to the first handler in the chain.
£60 is within the team lead's limit: approved here. It goes no further.
An expense of £700 goes to the first handler in the chain.
£700 is over the team lead's limit, so the team lead passes it to the next handler.
£700 is within the manager's limit: approved here. It goes no further.
A default handler at the end rejects or logs anything nobody handled. The same shape runs web middleware: authentication → rate limit → validation → handler.

sd6-t10.title: State: each mode is an object that knows what each event means

frames.caption: A vending machine reacts to the same button differently depending on its mode. Each mode is a State class that handles every event and decides the next state.
Idle + "select an item": not allowed yet. The Idle state answers with a clear message instead of doing something wrong.
Idle + "insert coin": valid. Idle handles it and moves the machine to HasCoin.
HasCoin + "insert coin" again: this state already holds a coin, so it says so. Same event, different behaviour — no if/elif on a status variable anywhere.
HasCoin + "select": move to Dispensing, which drops the item and returns the machine to Idle.
Back to Idle, ready for the next customer. The machine just forwards every event to its current state object.

sd7-t1.title: Parking lot: strategies choose spots and prices; observers keep the boards right

frames.caption: Version 1 of the class design: ParkingLot, Spot, Vehicle, Ticket. Spots come in sizes S, M and L; spots 1 and 3 are already taken.
A car arrives at the gate. The spot-assignment STRATEGY looks for the smallest free spot a car fits: M or L, so not spot 2.
Spot 4 fits. It is marked taken in ONE atomic step — so a car at another gate can't be given the same spot at the same moment.
A ticket is issued for spot 4. The display board subscribes to spot changes (Observer), so its count updates by itself.
Exit: scan the ticket. The PRICING strategy works out the fee from the time parked; after payment, the spot is freed and the board updates again.

sd7-t2.title: An elevator using LOOK: sweep one way, then the other

frames.caption: The lift is at floor 3, going up. Requested stops: 8, 1, 5, 6. Serving them in the order they were pressed would zig-zag up and down the building.
LOOK: keep going in one direction, serving every stop on the way, then turn around — like a lift operator sweeping up and down. Order: 5 → 6 → 8 → 1.
Stop at floor 5.
Stop at floor 6.
Stop at floor 8.
No more stops above: turn around and sweep down to floor 1.
A controller hands each new hall call to the best lift — idle and near, or already moving towards that floor in the same direction. Each lift's state machine keeps the doors shut while moving.

sd7-t3.title: Splitwise: one balance per person, then settle with few payments

frames.caption: Keep ONE net balance per person: positive means they are owed money, negative means they owe. Everyone starts at zero.
Ana pays £80 for dinner for all four. Split equally, each share is £20: Ana is owed £60, everyone else owes £20.
Ben pays £30 for a taxi for himself, Cai and Dev: £10 each. Balances add up — and always sum to zero.
Simplify: match the biggest debtor with the biggest creditor. Dev pays Ana £30.
Repeat: Cai pays Ana £30.
Everyone is at zero after 2 payments, instead of a payment for every expense share.

sd7-t4.title: A vending machine as a chain of states

frames.caption: The machine is Idle. Each mode is a state class that knows what each event means.
Select item B2, price £1.20: Idle → ItemSelected.
Insert £1.00: still short of £1.20, so it stays in ItemSelected and waits for more.
Insert 50p: paid £1.50 ≥ £1.20 → HasMoney.
Dispensing: drop the item, give 30p change, and go back to Idle.
Cancel while in ItemSelected or HasMoney gives the money back and returns to Idle; an item with no stock left can't be selected at all.

sd7-t5.title: LRU cache: a hash map plus a doubly linked list, both O(1)

frames.caption: An LRU cache of capacity 3: a hash map finds any key's node in O(1); a doubly linked list keeps the keys in order of use.
put(A): insert a node at the front, and add it to the map.
put(B): insert a node at the front, and add it to the map.
put(C): insert a node at the front, and add it to the map.
get(A): the map finds it at once; move its node to the front — it is now the most recently used.
put(D): insert at the front. Now there are 4, one too many — drop the node at the back, B, the least recently used.
get(B): not in the map — it was evicted earlier. A miss.

sd7-t6.title: A matching engine fills by best price, then by time

frames.caption: The order book: sell orders above, cheapest nearest the middle; buy orders below. At the same price, the OLDEST order is first in line — price-time priority.
A buy order arrives: 20 shares at up to £102. It fills against the cheapest sell orders while their price is at or below £102.
Fill 5 at £101. 15 still to buy.
Fill 3 at £101 — the second £101 order, because it arrived later than the first. 12 still to buy.
Fill 10 at £102. 2 still to buy.
The next sell order is £104 — above the buy limit — so matching stops. The 2 left over rests in the book as a new buy order at £102.

sd8-t1.title: A URL shortener: unique codes on the write path, a cache on the read path

frames.caption: Shorten a URL: POST /urls with the long URL. Many stateless API servers sit behind a load balancer.
Each server reserves a whole RANGE of IDs from the allocator in advance — 125,000,000 to 125,999,999 — so there is no single counter to queue on.
It takes the next ID from its own range, 125,000,042, and turns it into Base62 (0–9, a–z, A–Z): "8sudI". Short, and unique without any check.
Store "8sudI" → the long URL in the links table, keyed by the code, and reply with the short link.
Someone opens /8sudI. Reads far outnumber writes, so the redirect path must be fast.
Check Redis first. Popular codes are almost always there: a hit, and the API replies 301 straight away.
On a miss, read the links table, put the result in Redis for next time, then redirect.
The click is recorded by dropping an event on a queue, so counting never slows the redirect. When the table outgrows one database, shard it by code.

sd8-t2.title: A rate limiter shared by every gateway

frames.caption: The rule, loaded from a config store and cached in each gateway: 10 requests a minute per user. The same user's requests may hit ANY gateway.
A request reaches gateway 1. The limiter checks and updates the user's counter in Redis in one atomic step (a Lua script): 8 → 9, under the limit.
Allowed: the request goes on to the service.
Another request lands on gateway 2. It updates the SAME counter: 9 → 10. Still allowed — because the count is shared, two gateways can't each allow 10.
The next one would make 11. Over the limit: 429 Too Many Requests, with Retry-After. If Redis itself is down, the limiter fails open (or closed) by a rule you chose in advance.

sd8-t3.title: Notifications: one service, a queue per channel and priority

frames.caption: "Order shipped". The order service doesn't call any provider itself: it hands one event to the notification service.
The notification service checks the user's preferences (push yes, SMS no), applies per-user rate limits, and fills in the template.
It puts the message on a queue per channel and per priority — sign-in codes ahead of marketing — so a flood of emails can't delay a passcode.
A channel worker sends it to the push provider. The provider is slow and times out — so the worker retries with backoff.
Delivered. Every status is written to a delivery log; a message that keeps failing goes to a dead-letter queue. Idempotency keys stop a retry from notifying twice.

sd8-t4.title: Chat: store first, then route to wherever the recipient is connected

frames.caption: Every phone keeps a WebSocket open to a chat gateway. Alice sends Bob a message.
The gateway passes it to the chat service, which gives it a time-ordered ID and stores it — the message is safe before anyone is told.
Where is Bob connected? The registry says gateway 2.
The chat service pushes the message to gateway 2, which sends it down Bob's open connection. A "delivered" receipt travels back the same way.
Now Bob is offline: the registry has no gateway for him.
The message is already stored, so nothing is lost. The chat service asks the push service to send a notification to Bob's phone.
When Bob opens the app, he reconnects to some gateway and fetches everything newer than the last message he has, from the store.

sd8-t5.title: A news feed: push to followers' lists, pull for celebrities

frames.caption: Fan-out on write: Alice posts. The post is saved once in the post store.
Workers copy the post's ID into each follower's ready-made feed list (in Redis). Writing costs one entry per follower.
Reading is then trivial: Bob's feed is one list read, already in order. Post content comes from a cache, and photos from a CDN.
The celebrity problem: someone with millions of followers posts. Copying the ID into every feed would mean a huge burst of writes for one post.
Hybrid: push as normal for ordinary users, but DON'T fan out celebrity posts. They are only saved once.
When Bob reads, his ready-made feed is merged with the latest posts of the few celebrities he follows, pulled at read time. A ranking service can then reorder the result.

sd8-t6.title: Video: upload, transcode into segments, stream from a CDN

frames.caption: The app gets a pre-signed URL and uploads the video in parts, straight to object storage — never through your servers.
An event on a queue triggers transcoding workers.
They cut the video into short segments of a few seconds, and encode each one at several qualities. A manifest lists every segment for every quality.
Playback: the player fetches the manifest and segments from a CDN near the viewer, starting at a good quality.
The viewer's bandwidth drops. For the NEXT segment the player simply asks for a lower quality — no stall. That is adaptive bitrate. View counts are added up later, in the background.

sd8-t7.title: Ride hailing: search nearby cells, offer, lock

frames.caption: Drivers send their location every few seconds. Only the LATEST position is kept, in an in-memory geo index that splits the city into cells (geohashes).
A rider (R) asks for a car. Instead of measuring the distance to every driver in the city, search only the rider's cell and its neighbours.
Drivers in those cells are ranked by estimated arrival time: driver 3, driver 1, driver 2. The rest of the city is never looked at.
The trip is offered to driver 3 first, with a timeout. No answer in time…
…so it is offered to driver 1, who accepts. Their status is set to "on a trip" in one atomic update, so they can't be double-booked. A trip state machine takes over from here.

sd8-t8.title: Payments: idempotency keys, a ledger, and reconciliation

frames.caption: Checkout asks to charge £30, sending an idempotency key, k-91. The payment service creates a PENDING record; a UNIQUE constraint on the key means there can only ever be one.
It calls the payment provider, which handles the card details — you never store raw card numbers.
The call times out. Was the card charged or not? Unknown. Checkout retries — with the SAME key.
The unique key finds the existing payment, so the service does NOT charge again — it returns the current status. No double charge.
The provider's webhook arrives: succeeded. In ONE transaction the status becomes SUCCEEDED and balanced double-entry ledger rows are written. An outbox event tells the order service.
Every night a reconciliation job compares your ledger with the provider's settlement file, and flags anything that doesn't match.

sd8-t9.title: Autocomplete: walk the prefix; the answer is already stored there

frames.caption: Searches are logged and counted. The serving side is an in-memory trie: each node is a prefix, and each node STORES its top completions, worked out in advance.
The user types "c". Walk one step down from the root…
…"ca": one more step. The node already holds the answer — car, cat — so no subtree search is needed at request time.
The data pipeline runs offline: count the logged searches every hour or day, rebuild the trie, and swap the new one in. Clients wait for a pause in typing, and common prefixes are cached at the edge.

sd8-t10.title: A leaderboard on a sorted set: updates and ranks in log time

frames.caption: Scores live in a Redis sorted set: members kept in score order, so finding the top N or anyone's rank takes logarithmic time — no sorting on every request.
Noa scores 140 points. The game service saves the score durably, then updates the sorted set (ZINCRBY). Noa's entry moves up on its own — nothing else is re-sorted.
Top 3: ZREVRANGE 0 2 reads the first three members straight off the top.
Noa's rank: ZREVRANK gives 1, counting from 0 — so Noa is #2. Keep a separate set per period (daily, weekly) with an expiry.

sd8-t11.title: A distributed cache: hash to a node, replicate, fail over

frames.caption: The client library hashes each key onto a consistent-hash ring (with virtual nodes) to find its node — no central lookup.
user:42 hashes to node B. Each node is an in-memory hash table with LRU eviction and TTL expiry.
Each shard is copied to a replica, so a node's data isn't lost with it.
Node B dies. Cluster membership (from a config service, or gossip between nodes) marks it down, and its replica takes over its keys.
Adding a node moves only a small share of keys — the consistent-hashing property. Very hot keys get extra copies, and a lock stops a stampede of misses all reloading the same key.

sd9-t1.title: RAG: index the documents, then retrieve, re-rank and answer with sources

frames.caption: Ingestion runs whenever a document changes. First, parse it — PDF, wiki page, slides — into plain text.
Clean it, then split it into chunks of a few hundred words, overlapping a little so no idea is cut in half.
Turn each chunk into an embedding — a vector of numbers where similar meanings sit close together.
Store the vectors in a vector store, WITH metadata: the source, and who is allowed to see it. When the document changes, the whole pipeline runs again for it.
A question arrives: "How many days of leave do I get?" First rewrite it using the conversation so far, so it stands on its own.
Hybrid retrieval: vector search (meaning) plus keyword search (exact terms), filtered to documents THIS user may see.
A re-ranker scores the candidates more carefully, and the best few chunks go into the prompt.
The LLM streams an answer that cites its sources [1][2]. Retrieved text is checked for prompt injection, every step is traced, and a golden set of questions is re-run to catch regressions.

shapes.text: "25 days a year [1], plus bank holidays [2]."

sd9-t2.title: Recommendations: a cheap wide net, then a careful ranking

frames.caption: Scoring millions of items for every request with a heavy model is far too slow. So recommendations come in stages.
Candidate generation: quickly gather about 1,000 items from several cheap sources — embedding similarity (approximate nearest neighbours), "bought together", popular items.
Ranking: a richer model scores just those candidates, using user, item and context features from a feature store.

Re-ranking applies business rules — variety, freshness, nothing already seen — and the top 10 are shown. Every impression and click is logged to train the next model, and A/B tests measure the real effect.

sd9-t3.title: Fraud scoring in real time, and learning from the outcomes

frames.caption: A £950 card payment must be approved or stopped in milliseconds. It goes to a scoring service.
Real-time features are fetched from a feature store, kept fresh by a stream processor: 6 payments in the last 10 minutes, 4,000 km from the usual place, a new device.
Hand-written rules and an ML model (often gradient-boosted trees) both look at the features. The model scores this one 0.91.
Thresholds turn the score into a decision, tuned by what each mistake costs: above 0.9 block; 0.6–0.9 send to an analyst; below that approve. This one is blocked and queued for review.
Every decision and its features are logged. Weeks later, chargebacks arrive as the true labels; they are joined to the log to retrain the model, and drift is watched.

sd9-t4.title: LLM serving: keep the GPUs busy, route and scale per model

frames.caption: A GPU serves several requests at once, in a batch — here 4 slots. Each answer takes a different number of decoding steps.
Static batching: requests A–D start together. Short ones finish early, but their slots sit idle until the LONGEST one is done.
Only then can E and F start. Everything is done after 9 steps, with a lot of wasted GPU time.

Continuous batching: the moment any request finishes, a waiting one takes its slot. Same work, done after 6 steps — and short requests aren't stuck behind long ones. A paged KV cache makes the memory side of this work.
The gateway authenticates each team, enforces quotas and rate limits, and routes each request to a pool of servers for the right model.
Easy requests can go to a small, cheap model; hard ones to the large model.
Each pool scales on queue length and latency. Responses stream back token by token; repeated system prompts reuse cached work (prefix caching).

sd9-t5.title: An ML pipeline: validate, train, compare, deploy carefully, watch

frames.caption: An orchestrated pipeline (Airflow, say) replaces "someone copies the model file". It starts by ingesting new data.
Validate the data before training on it: missing columns, odd values, a sudden drop in rows. Bad data would stop the pipeline here — not after a bad model ships.
Features come from a feature store: one definition per feature, used for training (with point-in-time correct joins) and for serving — so the two never disagree.
Train, then evaluate against the model in production. Only a better model is registered.
Deploy carefully — a canary takes a small share of traffic first — then monitor data drift, prediction drift and business metrics.
When drift is detected (or on a schedule), the whole pipeline runs again: retraining is a loop, not a one-off.
